newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - T-notes face up to stocks' challenge.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - T-notes face up to stocks' challenge.

text.p: Share and bond prices on both sides of the Atlantic have hurtled to fresh peaks but U.S. Treasuries may be the safest bet ahead of nerve-wracking testimony from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan next week, analysts said on Thursday.

Although U.S. yields, which move in the opposite direction to prices, are now looking decidedly meagre compared to the sizzling stock market, an almost idyllic environment of strong growth and low inflation should allow investors to continue to reap chunky real returns.
"From a policy nexus, I would be more comfortable at this stage to be long bonds than long stocks," Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist Europe at BankAmerica in London.
In Europe, however, analysts favoured stocks as continental economies lumber to life and the road to monetary union throws up potential pitfalls for bonds.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average cracked the 8,000 barrier on Wednesday, ending up 63.17 points at 8,038.88, while the yield on the 30-year long bond slid through 6.5 percent for the first time since December last year.
British, German and French stock markets all scored record highs on Wednesday before succumbing to profit-taking on Thursday.

The catalyst for the gains was benign inflation data from the U.S. core consumer prices, excluding volatile food and energy prices, which rose at an annual rate of 2.4 percent in the first half of the year -- the slowest pace since 1965.
Expectations of a U.S. interest rate rise in August faded away.
European inflation also remains restrained as economies -- apart from Britain -- remain well behind the U.S. in the recent cycle.

Against such a background, real yields of around 4.1 percent on the U.S. long bond were not inconsiderable, Hawkins said. "Real yields may not have changed all that much simply since we've seen a ratcheting down of inflationary expectations."

And with Greenspan set to deliver his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on monetary policy and economic conditions to a House Banking subcommittee on Tuesday, stocks were looking a bit reckless at such heights, Hawkins said.
Markets will be waiting to see if Greenspan comes anywhere near repeating his warning about irrational exuberance in markets that sent stocks and bonds diving in December.

"I don't think (Greenspan) will be overly concerned about the improvement in longer dated yields because part of his job is to ensure an environment which allows as low cost funding for the Treasury as possible," Hawkins said. "But I think he will be concerned about the speculative bubble in the equity market."
David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Sterns International in London, saw the long bond slinking to 6.25 percent in the next one to two months but said in Europe, stocks were a better bet.
"There's a much stronger argument to buy stocks over bonds in Europe because its the bond markets have been making all the convergence gains in the last couple of years," he said.
He notes 10-year German yields at 5.54 percent are approaching their all-time low of 5.23 percent hit in April 1986 while European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) remains a potential minefield.
"What will be bad news for bonds is going to be good news for stocks," he said. "If EMU austerity comes to an end it's going to be a positive reason to be stuck into the European stock market."
Michael Burke, bond strategist at Citibank in London, however, hesitated to stand in the way of the surging U.S. stock market in favour of bonds.
"It's only when the liquidity tap is turned off is the overvaluation going to go into reverse," he said.
He notes one-year T-bill yields at 5.49 percent are now trading below the 5.50 percent federal funds target rate.
